stories.title: Sarawak's chip design firm SMD eyes 2030 IPO
stories.summary: State-owned Sarawak Microlectronics Design (SMD) is slated for commercialisation and is planning an initial public offering (IPO) as early as 2030.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.title_zh: 砂拉越芯片设计公司SMD瞄准2030年IPO
stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 4): State-owned Sarawak Microlectronics Design (SMD) is slated for commercialisation and is planning an initial public offering (IPO) as early as 2030.

According to the Sarawak Semiconductor Roadmap 2030, SMD is looking to attract at least RM2 billion in investments and create over 195,000 new jobs and 3,000 new high-skilled occupations.

SMD, launched in 2022, is a design company focused on higher-value chip design — particularly for renewable energy and digital infrastructure applications — as part of the state's "Silicon Longhouse" vision to build a holistic semiconductor ecosystem.

According to the roadmap, the semiconductor sector, led by SMD, is expected to contribute RM30 billion to the GDP of the state from 2030.

SMD is developing keteq.ai — an embedded AI offering real-time fault correction in power systems — and a GaN (gallium nitride) compound semiconductor power module that can be heterogeneously integrated with it for energy grids, renewables and data centres, in collaboration with the UK's CSA Catapult and 5G3i, currently in the commercial-readiness phase.

SMD is co-developing an advanced microcontroller for automotive applications, leveraging an existing Melexis automotive microcontroller IP used for control, data processing and communication in engine control units, flight control systems, navigation systems and more.

"Melexis’ vast experience in designing compound semiconductor ICs for automotive sector, paves the way into aerospace sector due to the similarity in IC requirements and usage for these sectors," read the blueprint.

SMD's Electronic Embedded System (Etes) initiatives include Sarapeg 2.0, a smart land marker that integrates GPS and/or sensor microchips into Sarapeg land markers with applications built on land marker data under SDG 15 (Life On Land), alongside the development of a cloud-based AI-enabled GIS known as next-gen e-Lasis.

stories.title: Oracle scraps US$7 billion deal to lease chips to Tencent under Trump pressure, FT reports
stories.summary: US officials have approached the firm to raise concerns about the deal, the newspaper says
stories.title_zh: Oracle在特朗普压力下取消向Tencent出租芯片的70亿美元交易
stories.content:
US officials have approached the firm to raise concerns about the deal, the newspaper says

\[BENGALURU\] Oracle has cancelled a multibillion-dollar chip leasing contract with Tencent after bowing to pressure from the Trump administration, the *Financial Times* reported on Wednesday (Nov 4).

US officials approached Oracle to raise concerns about the Tencent deal, the newspaper said, citing people familiar with the matter.

Tencent also received visits from top officials in Guangdong, where the group is based, who asked the company to support domestic Chinese chips, the report said.

Reuters could not immediately verify the report. Oracle, Tencent and the White House did not respond to Reuters requests for comment on the report.

The *Financial Times* reported in October that Tencent signed its largest overseas lease deal, worth an estimated US$7 billion, with Oracle

The deal would have given Tencent access to about 100,000 advanced artificial intelligence chips that were not available in China due to curbs from Washington and Beijing, according to the report.

Tencent had agreed to a five-year lease across multiple Oracle data centres in South-east Asia, according to the report.

This comes as Chinese AI developers are renting access to AI accelerators that are not available in their home country, such as those from American firm Nvidia, to avert US export controls.

Chinese tech companies are among the biggest customers of data centres in South-east Asia. REUTERS, BLOOMBERG

stories.title: Goodman, Digital Realty raid NextDC's register for $940m stake
stories.summary: Goodman Group and Digital Realty have jointly acquired a $940 million stake in NextDC, one of Australia's largest data center operators, by purchasing shares from the company's register. The investment combines Goodman's property development expertise with Digital Realty's global data center platform to expand in the Australian market.
stories.why_it_matters: This strategic alliance signals intensifying competition for Australian data center assets as AI demand converges with the country's renewable energy advantages. NextDC gains formidable development and global interconnection capabilities, while the entry of two major international players pressures local operators like Macquarie Telecom and may accelerate consolidation in a market previously dominated by domestic champions.

stories.title: AI-linked stocks slide in Asia as early US election results favour Democrats
stories.summary: South Korean and Taiwanese stocks tumbled on Wednesday as early US midterm election results pointed to strong Democratic gains, stoking worries that stricter oversight of data-centre projects could weigh on artificial intelligence (AI) investment.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.title_zh: 美国早期选举结果利好民主党，亚洲AI相关股票下跌
stories.content:
BENGALURU (Nov 4): South Korean and Taiwanese stocks tumbled on Wednesday as early US midterm election results pointed to strong Democratic gains, stoking worries that stricter oversight of data-centre projects could weigh on artificial intelligence (AI) investment.

Tech-heavy benchmarks bore the brunt of the selling, with South Korea's Kospi falling 4%, while Taiwan's benchmark index lost 3.3%, hitting its lowest level since late July.

The weakness also dragged MSCI's emerging markets index down 1.8% to levels not seen since early April.

The US midterm election outcome could help to shape several key market themes, from the pace of AI data-centre expansion and the fiscal outlook to defence spending and regulatory oversight of sectors like healthcare, banking and cryptocurrencies.

Growing public opposition to data-centre projects and efforts by some Democratic candidates to curb their expansion over concerns about electricity costs and environmental impact lend credence to those fears, said Inki Cho, a senior financial market strategist at Exness, an online trading platform.

South Korean chipmakers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics fell 6.1% and 4.1% respectively, while Taiwan's TSMC was down 2.2%.

Meanwhile, emerging Asian currencies broadly strengthened as the dollar fell sharply, led by a 0.5% gain in the South Korean won, while the ringgit and the Philippine peso each inched about 0.1% higher.

In Singapore, the dollar added 0.2%, while stocks fell 1.4%, extending a losing streak to a fifth consecutive session.

United Overseas Bank reported quarterly profit that missed analysts' expectations; its shares fell 6.5%.

Other banking heavyweights also declined, with DBS Group and Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp (OCBC) down 1.8% and 2.5% respectively. Investors looked ahead to DBS' third-quarter earnings, which are due on Thursday, and OCBC's results on Friday.

"Singapore bank stocks are increasingly vulnerable to profit-taking as investor expectations remain elevated," said James Ooi, the chief market strategist of Tiger Brokers.

"The key concern is whether Singapore banks can sustain profitability and returns on equity amid narrowing interest margins and moderating fee income."

In Indonesia, the rupiah was flat while stocks pared some of their earlier losses but were still down 0.6%, as investors assessed the financial regulator's newly announced sanctions for stock market violations.

The regulator said the measures included the closure of more than a dozen securities accounts linked to market misconduct.

Investor sentiment has been fragile since MSCI warned that Indonesia could be removed from a suite of widely tracked indices, prompting authorities to roll out support measures following the market's worst two-day sell-off on record.

"Despite undemanding valuations, investor focus is shifting to policy execution, market reforms and stronger enforcement," said Ari Jahja, the head of Indonesia research at Macquarie Capital.

Elsewhere, Thai stocks fell more than 1.1%, sending the benchmark to its lowest level since late April, while the baht edged higher against the dollar.

Separately, the country's finance minister said Thailand had no plans to raise the country's public debt ceiling.

- Indonesian 10-year benchmark yields stood at 7.707%
- Democrats were closing in on the US House, making gains in the Senate
- China's yuan hit a two-week low as investors weighed the central bank's foreign exchange reserve hike

stories.title: Govt to ensure existing industries not affected by power supply to data centres, says Johari Ghani
stories.summary: Malaysian Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani has assured that data center development will not compromise electricity supply to existing industrial sectors that form the backbone of Malaysia's economy. The statement comes amid rising concerns that data center power demand could strain national grid capacity and affect other manufacturers.
stories.why_it_matters: This government intervention reveals acute political tension as Malaysia's data center gold rush—attracting billions in investment—collides with finite grid capacity and existing industrial stakeholders. The minister's promise will be tested by the aggregate power demands of approved projects, potentially forcing trade-offs between data center growth speed, renewable energy buildout timelines, and protection of Malaysia's manufacturing competitiveness.

stories.title_zh: Johari Ghani：政府将确保现有产业不受数据中心供电影响
stories.summary_zh: 马来西亚投资、贸易和工业部长 Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani 保证，data center 发展不会损害构成马来西亚经济支柱的现有工业部门的电力供应。这一声明是在人们日益担忧 data center 电力需求可能使国家电网容量紧张并影响其他制造商的背景下发表的。
stories.why_zh: 这一政府干预揭示了随着马来西亚的 data center 淘金热——吸引数十亿美元投资——与有限的电网容量和现有工业利益相关者发生碰撞，政治紧张局势日益尖锐。部长的承诺将受到已批准项目总电力需求的考验，可能迫使在 data center 增长速度、可再生能源建设时间表和保护马来西亚制造业竞争力之间做出权衡。
stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 4): The government will ensure that the development of data centres will not affect electricity supply to existing industries which form the backbone of Malaysia’s national economy, said Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani.

He said data centres are important infrastructure to support the adoption of future technologies, but their development must not disrupt existing industrial sectors' energy needs.

He said data centre developments must be balanced to ensure electricity supply to existing industries remains protected.

“We will not interfere with the existing industries as they are the backbone of our economy. However, we also need to be involved in data centres as they represent future technology that needs to be adopted in various activities across our industries,” he told reporters after officiating the Amazon Web Services Cloud and AI Day programme here on Wednesday.

Johari said the development of data centres is necessary because the technology will be used across industries, including manufacturing, which is increasingly shifting towards more advanced technologies.

Malaysia therefore has to provide adequate infrastructure to enable companies to adopt and develop new technological solutions, he said.

Johari said the government will ensure data centre infrastructure benefits foreign investors and also creates opportunities for local companies to participate in its supply chain.

He said the government has stipulated a minimum of 30% local content in data centre development, to include the use of local consultants, contractors, engineers and procurement managers.

On infrastructure development financing, Johari said the government encourages foreign investors to bring in capital to develop these facilities.

This approach allows investors to bear the cost of developing data centres, while Malaysia benefits from the facilities provided and the economic opportunities created, he said.

“They (foreign investors) come with investments to develop this infrastructure. They provide the capital, but we reap the benefits,” he said.

He said Malaysia also has the capacity to support data centre development through its energy resources, including natural gas, and the development of renewable energy sources.

Johari said such infrastructure development is important to ensure Malaysia adopts new technologies and enhances productivity across economic sectors.

stories.title: Planning vital to prevent electricity system constraints, says Fadillah
stories.summary: Deputy Prime Minister Datuk Seri Fadillah Yusof has called for timely decisions, coordinated planning and the ability to deliver infrastructure on the electricity system before constraints begin to hold back the country’s growth.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.title_zh: Fadillah：规划对于防止电力系统瓶颈至关重要
stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 4): Deputy Prime Minister Datuk Seri Fadillah Yusof has called for timely decisions, coordinated planning and the ability to deliver infrastructure on the electricity system before constraints begin to hold back the country’s growth.

He said there should also be greater flexibility in power flows across Peninsular Malaysia which will help the government to respond to changing demand patterns, accommodate new power generation and support the integration of renewable energy.

Malaysia’s electrical system should keep pace as industries expand and the economy becomes increasingly digital, more so since energy security is fundamental to Malaysia’s development and economic resilience, he said.

“The infrastructure we develop today must serve the needs of tomorrow,” he said when officiating the CGNEI Gas Turbine Power Committee 2026 Work Conference at the Edra Melaka Power Plant (EMPP) in Melaka on Wednesday.

Fadillah, who is also the energy transition and water transformation minister, stressed that every investment and technological advancement should ultimately translate into meaningful benefits for the people whom the government serves.

Gas turbine technology continues to play an important role in Malaysia’s power generation landscape.

Its ability to provide dependable electricity and operational flexibility helps support grid stability and complement the growing contribution of variable renewable energy.

“We must also remain mindful of the uncertainties around us. Geopolitical tensions, fuel price volatility, supply chain disruptions and climate-related risks can affect both the availability and cost of energy,” he said.

“These challenges demand careful judgement as we work to maintain security of supply, protect affordability and advance our climate commitments,” he said.

The deputy prime minister also highlighted that peak electricity demand in the peninsula could increase substantially within less than a decade.

Citing government growth projections, he cautioned they indicate that peak electricity demand in the peninsula could rise from 21.3 gigawatts in 2026 to 33.5 gigawatts by 2035.

“This is a substantial increase in less than a decade,” he said.

Fadillah pointed out that Malaysia’s growing role in data centres, artificial intelligence, semiconductor manufacturing and other high-value industries presents considerable opportunities and challenges.

“These investments can create quality employment, strengthen local enterprises and advance our technological capabilities.

“They also place greater demands on our electricity system and supporting infrastructure,” he said, adding that emerging data centre developments in Melaka illustrate this need clearly.

He said the opportunities being explored through collaboration between Melaka Corporation (MCorp) and Edra reinforce the importance of aligning digital investment with the availability of electricity, grid capacity, water and other essential utilities.

This entails investments across the electricity system, from generation to transmission and distribution.

He emphasised that a new power plant can fulfil its purpose only when the wider network can deliver its electricity safely and efficiently to where it is needed.

To this end, the government places strong emphasis on strengthening the capacity and resilience of the national grid.

Sustained attention on grid development, digitalisation and demand-side management are needed, he said.

“Our responsibility is to turn this direction into delivery. That means clear implementation milestones, sound governance and close coordination between government and industry.

“It also means having the humility to review our assumptions as circumstances change, while remaining steadfast in the outcomes we seek for our nation,” said Fadillah.

stories.content:
Malaysia’s Perak State Development Corporation (PKNPk) and Global Vision Lab Sdn Bhd (GVL) are exploring a proposed artificial intelligence data center (AIDC) development in Perak with planned capacity exceeding 100MW, according to PKNPk press release yesterday.

To date, only a non-disclosure agreement and a letter of consent have been signed; as such more specific details like the full scope is not available.

Under the agreement, PKNPk will handle state-level stakeholders while GVL is responsible for development planning and preliminary assessments.

“The initiative supports the aspirations of Perak Sejahtera 2030 and creates opportunities for Perak to emerge as a destination for the development of high-technology digital infrastructure,” said PKNPk chief executive Datuk Redza Rafiq.

Perak is a state that lies north of Selangor state and Klang Valley where Kuala Lumpur and Cyberjaya, the current data center hubs are located in central Peninsular Malaysia.

stories.title: Taiwan's AI chip role grows as HCLTech spotlights ecosystem
stories.summary: HCLTech has highlighted Taiwan's growing importance in the AI chip ecosystem as the industry shifts from discrete chip design toward integrated system-level solutions. Taiwanese foundries led by TSMC and server manufacturers like Foxconn and Wistron are increasingly central to assembling the complete AI hardware stacks demanded by hyperscalers.
stories.why_it_matters: Taiwan's evolution from component supplier to system integrator captures more value per AI server and deepens its irreplaceability in global supply chains, even as geopolitical risks intensify. For APAC data center operators, this concentration means that disruptions—whether from earthquakes, trade restrictions, or military tensions—would have amplified cascading effects on AI capacity deployment timelines and costs.
stories.title_zh: 随着 HCLTech 聚焦生态系统，Taiwan 的 AI chip 角色日益增强
stories.summary_zh: HCLTech 强调了台湾在 AI 芯片生态系统中日益增长的重要性，因为行业正从离散芯片设计转向集成系统级解决方案。以 TSMC 为首的台湾代工厂和 Foxconn、Wistron 等服务器制造商，在组装 hyperscaler 所需的完整 AI 硬件堆栈方面正变得越来越核心。
stories.why_zh: 台湾从零部件供应商向系统集成商的演进，使其在每个 AI 服务器上获取更多价值，并加深其在全球供应链中的不可替代性，即使地缘政治风险加剧。对于 APAC data center 运营商而言，这种集中意味着无论是地震、贸易限制还是军事紧张局势造成的中断，都将对 AI 容量部署时间表和成本产生放大的连锁效应。
stories.content:
Wed, 4th Nov 2026 (Today)
HCLTech has published research on Taiwan's role in global AI semiconductor infrastructure.

The study, prepared by Omdia, positions Taiwan at the centre of manufacturing and system integration for the next phase of AI build-out.

The white paper argues that competition in AI semiconductors is shifting away from standalone chip speed towards integrated platforms that combine compute, memory, connectivity, packaging and software. This, it says, is increasing the importance of regions that can pair chip production with assembly, testing and server manufacturing.

Taiwan features heavily in that assessment. Taiwan-headquartered foundries account for more than half of the global foundry services market, while Taiwanese original design manufacturers produce about 90% of the world's server motherboards and 80% of server systems, according to the research.

Omdia says TSMC accounts for more than 90% of the world's leading-edge semiconductor production, underlining how concentrated advanced manufacturing remains on the island. The report links that position to Taiwan's growing relevance in building large-scale AI systems, not just producing individual chips.

### Platform shift

The study describes a semiconductor market being reshaped by the demands of AI models and data centre infrastructure. As architectures grow more complex, performance increasingly depends on how multiple elements work together across a system.

That includes not just silicon design, but memory integration, advanced packaging, interconnects, power delivery and software. In that context, the paper identifies system-level coordination as an increasingly important driver of commercial success in AI hardware.

“AI semiconductor competition is no longer about who builds the fastest chip, but who delivers the best workload outcome. Performance now depends on compute, memory, packaging, connectivity and software being designed together from the start. That makes execution the real differentiator - the leaders will be those who can turn complex silicon ambition into scalable, production-ready platforms,” said Ameer Saithu, executive vice president and global head of semiconductor business, HCLTech.

### Packaging focus

Advanced packaging is identified as one of the most significant parts of that shift. The white paper highlights TSMC's CoWoS technology as an example of how high-performance logic and high-bandwidth memory can be combined within more complex AI systems.

Taiwan's position in packaging extends beyond TSMC. The report notes that ASE Technology Holding, a Taiwan-based outsourced semiconductor assembly and test provider, holds roughly 40% of the global OSAT market.

This matters because AI infrastructure is no longer confined to chips in isolation. Large deployments increasingly require close coordination between processors, memory, networking, thermal design and physical system assembly.

As an illustration of that trend, the white paper cites NVIDIA's GB200 NVL72, which integrates 72 GPUs and 36 CPUs in a single liquid-cooled rack. The example is intended to show the scale of current AI systems and the engineering demands involved in bringing them together.

### Regional spread

While the report presents Taiwan as the principal hub, it also describes a broader Asian semiconductor network that is becoming more distributed. Singapore, Malaysia, Vietnam and China are all identified as contributors across manufacturing, packaging, testing and equipment production.

That regional spread is helping add capacity and resilience to semiconductor supply chains, the study says. Even so, it argues that Taiwan remains the main link between advanced manufacturing, integration and the industrialisation of AI infrastructure.

HCLTech's Taiwan leadership echoed that point in comments accompanying the publication. “Taiwan's role in AI goes well beyond making chips. Its depth, from wafers to racks, spanning leading-edge manufacturing, advanced packaging and server production, is very hard to replicate. Even as capacity spreads across Asia, Taiwan remains the centre that connects it all, and the opportunity now is to turn that strength into faster, more resilient AI deployment,” said Terry Tai, country head of Taiwan, HCLTech.

The paper also points to growing investment by hyperscale companies in custom AI silicon, a trend that could deepen reliance on Taiwan's ecosystem. The combination of foundry scale, packaging expertise and server production gives the market a role in both design and deployment.

“As hyperscalers accelerate investment in custom AI silicon, Taiwan's semiconductor ecosystem is becoming even more important to the global AI infrastructure value chain. HCLTech combines its global silicon engineering experience with a deep understanding of Taiwan's semiconductor ecosystem to help customers turn increasingly complex AI chip designs into scalable, manufacturable products. Working closely alongside customers' engineering teams gives us a practical view of what it takes to move from design intent to volume production,” said Hong Ming Chang, senior director, Taiwan, HCLTech.

stories.title: Cooler servers, cheaper batteries, automated sandblasting: How Singapore firms put RIE support to work
stories.summary: Home-grown businesses are using the S$37 billion in the R&D kitty to take new technologies from lab to market
stories.title_zh: 更冷的服务器、更便宜的电池、自动化喷砂：新加坡企业如何将RIE支持投入实际应用
stories.content:
Home-grown businesses are using the S$37 billion in the R&D kitty to take new technologies from lab to market

\[SINGAPORE\] From equipment that gives aerospace and oil-and-gas components a consistent finish and liquid cooling for data centres to batteries designed to store electricity for longer periods, three Singapore companies are turning research into commercial products.

*The Business Times* met the leaders of Abrasive Engineering, Hyprcool and VFT, whose R&D efforts have received support under Singapore’s Research, Innovation and Enterprise (RIE) plans.

Singapore has committed S$37 billion to research and innovation under its next plan, RIE2030.

The first report card on RIE2025 showed business R&D spending rose 64 per cent to S$9 billion between 2018 and 2023; it also flagged scope to generate more commercial value from public-sector research.

## Abrasive Engineering fights obsolescence

Tan Ser Hean believes that enthusiasm alone cannot sustain a business. Even successful companies must keep innovating to meet demand, he said, or risk “closing shop very fast”.

“For a SME (small and medium-sized enterprise), it’s about survival,” said the executive chairman of surface-finishing equipment maker Abrasive Engineering. “It’s no use having passion if you cannot survive.”

His answer is to invest in R&D, which he said will give the business technology essential for its long-term survival.

The 71-year-old has handed day-to-day management of the company he founded in 1990 to the next generation. But rather than give them money, he is working on giving them technology instead by developing solutions that improve productivity and equip them to carry the company forward.

Abrasive supplies equipment to major aerospace and oil-and-gas companies through its products which enable them to treat component surfaces consistently.

In 2010, the company spotted an opportunity to develop a magnetic valve to regulate the flow of metallic abrasives. At the time, Tan said, only one manufacturer, based in the US, made such valves.

Abrasive committed about S$500,000 of its own funds to the technology and completed its first functional prototype in 2016. Its system enables one controller to operate four valves, compared with one for the US product. It secured a US patent in 2021.

With the valve market acceptance, Tan was encouraged to develop more products. But having spent years on that valve, he wanted to move faster.

His solution lay in using a research institute with a team of scientists and research engineers. “If we can pull them together and develop things together, it will be so much faster,” he said.

In 2018, Abrasive began working with the Advanced Remanufacturing and Technology Centre (ARTC) of the Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A\*Star) and the National Metrology Centre (NMC) on a valve for non-ferrous abrasives.

The 18-month collaboration produced a proof of concept using microwave sensing. ARTC also supplied project management to keep research moving when Abrasive’s staff had to see to urgent customer orders.

The partnership grew into a joint laboratory in 2020, with a combined investment of S$5.5 million over three years to develop flow-control products and automated surface-treatment equipment.

The collaboration received support through research and innovation funding schemes under RIE2020 and RIE2025.

One project, with ARTC and robotics start-up Augmentus, developed a system that scans components and generates instructions for a robotic arm, reducing manual programming.

The first phase yielded six new product lines, including higher-flow valves and automated high-capacity sandblasting systems. Products developed in the lab generated S$3.5 million in revenue between 2020 and 2023, Tan said.

Annual revenue has doubled from S$6 million before the first joint laboratory to about S$12 million.

Further research addressed another vulnerability – dependence on a Japanese sensor supplier. In 2024 and 2025, Abrasive worked with ARTC and NMC to develop its own microwave sensor, incorporating it into products sold in 2025.

A second joint-lab phase launched in October 2025, under A\*Star’s S$21 million advanced manufacturing initiative involving several local SMEs, will support further product development and overseas expansion. Abrasive targets annual revenue of S$25 million by 2030.

While some small companies may feel safer keeping money in their pockets, Tan regards technology as an investment in growth, and enables his customers to improve productivity and achieve consistent results.

“You must spend money to acquire technology and develop new products. Then your company can grow,” he said. “If not, one day you will be obsolete.”

## Hyprcool puts liquid-cooling into real-world use

As data centres face growing scrutiny over their energy and water consumption, liquid-cooling technology firm Hyprcool is developing a more efficient way to manage heat generated by artificial intelligence workloads.

Founded by Greg Ong, the company has developed a spray-cooling technology that captures heat directly from server components, unlike conventional systems that use air-conditioning and chilled-water infrastructure to cool the space around servers.

Drawing on 19 years of tech experience and work in the data centre sector, Ong worked on the limitations of conventional cooling systems even as AI raised demand for computing power.

“Considering what we are experiencing in the world today with AI, those cooling demands are 10 to 15 times higher. It’s a tremendous amount of heat coming out of all these servers and the graphics processing units (GPUs) they run. You need a lot of electricity and water to keep up with it,” he said.

Hyprcool’s system uses 70 to 90 per cent less facility infrastructure than conventional systems. It also halves energy consumption, and water usage is “virtually zero”.

Its compact design allows deployment from offices, without dedicated computer rooms in full data centres, and minimal to no noise is generated, Ong added.

The company, which holds patents for its cooling technology in 30 countries, commercialised its first product in 2024.

Hyprcool is one of only three entities in Singapore conducting research into liquid cooling, but is the only one to have commercialised its technology, said Ong.

The firm began its research and development in 2018, working with A\*Star’s Singapore Institute of Manufacturing Technology and the Centre for Environmental Sustainability at Ngee Ann Polytechnic, funded by Enterprise Singapore (EnterpriseSG).

While Ong declined to disclose the amount of funding received, he said the collaboration gave the company access to engineering expertise and scientific knowledge that would have been difficult to source independently.

“Sometimes it’s not about the money. It’s the know-how, the expertise, the scientists who bring all this know-how to the table,” he said.

The collaboration helped Hyprcool understand the technical requirements of its cooling system, including the design and internal structure needed to achieve the expected performance.

While funding under the RIE plan supported its R&D, the development process was not without challenges.

The Covid-19 pandemic disrupted progress, and market inertia and unfamiliarity with alternative cooling technologies made it difficult to convince potential customers to move away from conventional systems.

“Everyone grew up in the air-cooling world. Now you’re asking them to go and relearn things. It can be very challenging,” he said.

Hyprcool is now exploring overseas markets and applications beyond conventional data centres.

Last year, it explored supplying a 300-megawatt data centre in the US, but found its manufacturing capacity insufficient to meet demand.

“They were talking about something 50 times larger than what we’re used to,” Ong said. “If they placed an order for a few thousand units, it might take me two years to deliver everything because we don’t have the correct manufacturing setup.”

Hyprcool plans to revisit the US market in the coming months, focusing on smaller data centres.

Meanwhile, the company began its first overseas deployment in Japan this year, where its product is being tested in a pilot project.

Hyprcool is also exploring opportunities in industrial computing, where AI is used in applications such as warehouse robots and cameras monitoring manufacturing processes.

“The challenge right now is that there is a very big market in industrial computing already happening … but they lack the performance of a data centre-grade AI server,” Ong said.

The company is looking to bridge this gap with systems that combine powerful GPU computing with local processing capabilities that would enable industrial users to run complex AI models on-site rather than rely on data centres.

The product is targeted for commercialisation in the third quarter of 2027.

## VFT uses waste to cut battery-pack costs

With Singapore’s demand for electricity expected to rise, energy-storage company VFT set out to make it cheaper to store power for longer by tapping R&D to lower the high upfront cost of its batteries.

The push comes as the growing demand for AI drives the expansion of power-hungry data centres, increasing the need for energy-storage capacity, said VFT chief executive Vidal Bharath.

Energy-storage solutions, such as flow batteries and lithium-ion battery packs, enable excess renewable energy to be stored for use after dark, without “having to turn on the fossil fuels later in the evening”, he said.

Founded in 2018 as VFlowTech, VFT develops vanadium redox flow batteries, which are now being used in places such as Pulau Ubin to support the island’s microgrid using a one-megawatt-hour system.

The batteries work by storing energy in a liquid containing the metal, which is pumped through a central cell stack to generate electricity.

One key difference between vanadium redox flow batteries and lithium-ion batteries lies in their lifespans, said Dr Bharath.

While conventional lithium-ion battery packs on power grids last between five and eight years, vanadium flow battery systems can be designed to last more than 20.

However, the higher upfront cost can deter customers from deploying flow batteries, he said.

Earlier this year, VFT’s vanadium redox flow battery packs cost up to US$500 per kilowatt hour, compared to about US$100 for lithium-ion battery packs.

While flow batteries are more cost-effective over a longer lifespan, government and commercial clients may be hesitant to pay substantially more upfront, said Dr Bharath.

The challenge, however, is that vanadium, a key component of flow batteries, is “really hard to extract”, and it accounts for the largest share of production expense.

He added that “getting the cost of vanadium down” is therefore the most important thing for his firm to focus on.

The company has pursued that goal since its founding in 2018**,** when it began collaborating with the Energy Research Institute @ Nanyang Technological University on commercialising vanadium redox flow battery technology.

More than eight years later, it launched a joint venture in 2026 with an Indian supplier to extract vanadium, a key input for its batteries, from petroleum-industry waste. The arrangement halved the cost of obtaining the metal and brought down battery-pack costs by more than 60 per cent, to US$175 a kilowatt hour.

VFT’s R&D projects received support through the Industry-Alignment Fund – Industry Collaboration Projects scheme under the RIE 2025 plan.

Separately, EnterpriseSG and the National Research Foundation supported its supply-chain integration with the Indian supplier.

The firm has also brought down costs through product standardisation, drawing on experience from pilot-scale projects in Singapore.

These included an installation with liquid storage logistics company Advario in Jurong Island and a project at Alkaff Kampung Melayu Mosque.

Dr Bharath said standardisation lets VFT scale up its battery systems using repeatable components, rather than “reinventing the wheel” for each project.

Beyond Singapore, VFT has about 10 gigawatt-hours’ worth of vanadium-specified tenders in the pipeline in Asia for the next 12 to 18 months.

Potential projects include supporting power grids in India, supplying long-duration energy storage for solar farms in the Middle East and working with customers in South-east Asia.

For Bharath, these opportunities are part of a broader goal to make “renewables more mainstream”.

“It’s not just about the renewables themselves; it’s about the infrastructure that allows them to happen,” he said. “It can’t be solar and wind during the day, then everyone turning back to fossil fuels at night. That’s the gap VFT bridges.”

stories.title: Trump proposes AI data centres generate own power
stories.summary: Former President Donald Trump suggested new, large-scale data centres should generate their own electricity and return excess to the grid. This proposal raises questions about existing energy strategies and equipment supply chains for developers.
stories.title_zh: 特朗普提议AI数据中心自发电
stories.content:
Former President Donald Trump has proposed that new, large-scale data centres should generate their own electricity and return any excess to the local community or grid. He also suggested developers make financial arrangements with host communities, including payments to residents.This position, if translated into formal policy, would challenge existing grid connections and power purchase agreements (PPAs) for data centre developers. Equipment availability for onsite power systems, including gas-fired, nuclear, and battery-backed components, is already constrained. Some turbine models are effectively sold out through 2031, according to Patrick Hughes, Senior Vice President of Strategy, Technical, and Industry Affairs at the National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA).
### Feasibility and Challenges

It is technically possible for a standalone AI data centre to provide its own power, whether through combined-cycle plants or solar plus storage, Hughes said. However, he noted it is not feasible for an entire fleet of AI data centres to supply 100 per cent of their own power and operate reliably 24/7. This would require significant operational management and maintenance.AI training and inference facilities have distinct power densities and load profiles compared to traditional data centres. The AI infrastructure buildout faces immense demand for electrical equipment and skilled labour across multiple sectors. Permitting timelines, fuel and equipment supply chains, interconnection rules, and community considerations also vary by location.
### Hybrid Solutions and Existing Commitments

A blanket onsite power requirement would also conflict with existing clean-energy mandates and corporate sustainability goals. Many AI data centres already have agreements to draw power from solar and wind projects. Developers may need a hybrid approach, combining onsite generation and storage with a grid connection, which the AI Data Center Energy Performance Framework accounts for.This framework offers technical standards and guiding principles for safety, resilience, and grid interaction. It supports flexible onsite and offsite energy strategies, including renewables and intelligent energy storage. Hughes stated that the optimal onsite generation strategy depends on each facility’s load, site, and regulatory landscape.

Princeton Digital Group (PDG), a leading data center operator in Asia Pacific, today said that it has secured approximately US$ 1.3 billion (\~RM 5.1 billion) in green financing for continued development and expansion of its JH1 campus in Johor, Malaysia. The loan contributed to part of the US$ 5 billion in debt financing that the firm planned to raise as announced in March to fund the delivery of contracted data center capacity across Asia Pacific.

Underwritten by six banks, namely Affin Bank, HSBC, Maybank, OCBC, Standard Chartered and UOB, the loan builds on the financing secured for earlier phases of the JH1 campus secured from three banks in April 2024, and subsequently upsized with four banks in October 2025.

“This financing reflects the confidence of our banking partners, several of whom have supported JH1 since its earliest phases, in PDG’s execution capabilities and deep hyperscaler partnerships,” said Rangu Salgame, Chairman, CEO and Co-Founder of PDG.

Located in Sedenak Tech Park, JH1 is a 200MW campus designed to support high-density AI and cloud workloads.

stories.title: Schneider Electric: AI racks to exceed 1MW with 800V DC power
stories.summary: Schneider Electric projects that AI server racks will exceed 1MW of power consumption as the industry adopts 800V DC power architectures, up from approximately 400kW today. The transition is expected to align with Nvidia's Rubin Ultra platform launch in 2027, representing a fundamental redesign of data center power infrastructure.
stories.why_it_matters: The leap to 1MW racks will obsolete much existing data center design and force wholesale infrastructure reinvestment across APAC's installed base, favoring new builds over retrofits. stories.title_zh: Schneider Electric：AI机架将采用800V DC电源突破1MW
stories.summary_zh: Schneider Electric 预计，随着行业采用 800V DC 电力架构，AI 服务器机架功率消耗将超过 1MW，高于目前的约 400kW。这一转变预计将与 2027 年 Nvidia Rubin Ultra 平台的推出相一致，代表 data center 电力基础设施的根本性重新设计。

stories.content:
AI racks are set to increase from approximately 400kW to at least 1MW as data centers transition to 800V direct current (DC) power architectures, according to Steve Carlini, chief AI advocate at Schneider Electric.Carlini told Capacity that 800V DC power will arrive with NVIDIA’s Rubin Ultra platform in 2027. Hyperscalers are expected to be the initial adopters before the technology becomes available to colocation providers and neoclouds.The move to 800V DC power is necessary because traditional alternating current (AC) power distribution can no longer efficiently supply the densest GPU racks. Carlini noted that physical limits have been reached, making it difficult to power each server with current copper sizes.The solution involves relocating power supplies from servers into a sidecar, which Schneider Electric calls its NetShelter power rack. This rack also incorporates batteries and capacitors to manage power draw fluctuations from GPU clusters, enabling tighter packing of server boards and GPUs.Carlini indicated there will not be a single 800V DC standard. NVIDIA’s design operates from 0V to 800V, while Mt Diablo, a project with Google and the Open Compute Project, uses plus and minus 400V. Battery and capacitor configurations will also vary.
### Power and Cooling Shifts

On the largest US projects, behind-the-meter power generation is becoming more common, with 50 to 100 per cent of total load sourced on site or from adjacent generation. Carlini observed growing demand for energy parks, primarily built around natural gas turbines.Schneider Electric supplies switchgear and software for these sites, which often parallel 50MW turbines into 200MW blocks. Carlini also highlighted a significant shift in cooling, with NVIDIA’s Rubin systems designed for liquid cooling at 45°C.This higher temperature allows many new liquid-cooled facilities to use dry coolers almost year-round, reducing reliance on chillers and cutting data center water use. Operators are also moving away from drinking water, recycling wastewater for cooling loops.
### Industry Trends and Challenges

Carlini expects prefabrication to become mainstream by late 2027, offering speed, predictability, and quality for rapidly changing rack densities. Factory-built power and cooling systems can be installed while facility work proceeds in parallel.He also pointed to faster utility grid queues in the US and Europe as a potential tipping point by late 2027. This could occur if utilities accelerate impact studies and clear speculative projects from the queue.Carlini anticipates enterprises will shift to right-sized AI stacks and dedicated models for specific applications. This change may lead to measuring data center capacity in 'tokens' alongside megawatts.

stories.title: Amogy to pilot ammonia cracking technology in Singapore
stories.summary: The pilot could help Singapore assess whether ammonia can be turned into reliable industrial hydrogen for data centres and heavy industry.
stories.title_zh: Amogy 将在 Singapore 试点 ammonia cracking 技术
stories.content:
Wed, 4th Nov 2026 (Today)
Amogy will pilot its ammonia cracking technology at the Low-Carbon Technology Translational Testbed on Jurong Island, in partnership with A\*STAR and with support from the Singapore Economic Development Board. The project makes Amogy one of the first partners at the new facility.

Amogy plans to deploy its ammonia cracking module in 2027. The unit is designed to produce up to one tonne of hydrogen a day under industrial operating conditions, with the data intended to inform larger deployments of ammonia-based hydrogen and power systems in Singapore.

The testbed, known as LCT3, is hosted at the A\*STAR Institute of Sustainability for Chemicals, Energy and Environment on Jurong Island. It is designed to bridge laboratory research and commercial use by giving companies a site to test low-carbon technologies at larger scale.

The agreement extends a partnership between Amogy and A\*STAR announced in 2025. That earlier tie-up focused on lowering emissions in sectors including data centres and heavy industry, while this new phase gives the collaboration a defined pilot project.

### Singapore plans

Beyond the pilot, the collaboration will cover research into lower-cost catalysts for ammonia-based hydrogen production. The Singapore work is also leading Amogy to establish its first research and development centre outside the US.

The move adds to the company's existing presence in Asia. Amogy is headquartered in New York and already operates in Singapore, Tokyo and Seoul, alongside its US sites.

Singapore's role in the project reflects the city-state's broader push to decarbonise industry on Jurong Island and assess alternative fuels for energy-intensive sectors. It also aligns with efforts to examine how low-carbon ammonia and hydrogen could support power supply for new data centre capacity.

Rules for Singapore's second data centre call for applications required at least 50% of proposed new capacity to be powered through eligible green energy pathways, including low-carbon ammonia and hydrogen. That has drawn attention to technologies that can convert imported fuels into usable low-carbon energy on site.

Amogy's system centres on cracking ammonia into hydrogen and nitrogen. In this pilot, the company will provide its reformer and catalyst technologies and oversee project execution, while A\*STAR will support testing and joint development work.

### Industrial testing

The emphasis of the Jurong Island deployment is not on a laboratory demonstration, but on operating the system under industrial conditions. That distinction matters for companies and policymakers assessing whether ammonia can serve as a practical hydrogen carrier for large energy users.

"Singapore is a strategic hub for Amogy's work across Asia-Pacific, where we are strengthening our core R&D capabilities and building our commercial presence," said Seonghoon Woo, Chief Executive Officer, Amogy. "Building on our multi-year collaboration with A\*STAR and with the support of EDB, deploying our ammonia cracking module on Jurong Island is about putting our technology to work at a meaningful scale and laying the groundwork for broader commercial adoption across the region, including industrial hydrogen applications and data center power."

A\*STAR said the pilot is intended to address a central issue facing newer low-carbon energy systems: proving they can work reliably beyond the research stage.

"For emerging low-carbon energy technologies, a critical challenge is demonstrating that they can perform reliably at scale and under industrial conditions. This is particularly relevant for technologies that use ammonia as a hydrogen carrier. Our collaboration with Amogy and real-world testing at LCT3 aims to bridge the gap between promising research and industrial adoption, building confidence in their potential for wider deployment," said Professor Lim Keng Hui, Assistant Chief Executive Officer, Science & Engineering Research Council, A\*STAR.

Singapore's investment promotion agency cast the project as part of a broader strategy to attract companies that can use the country's research base as a route into regional markets.

"Amogy's collaboration with A\*STAR demonstrates how companies can tap on Singapore's strong research capabilities to advance promising low carbon solutions towards industrial application. We welcome Amogy's plans to deepen its R&D presence in Singapore and use Singapore as a base to pursue growth opportunities across the region," said Mr Wey-Len Lim, Executive Vice President, Singapore Economic Development Board.

stories.title: Melbourne cheaper than Sydney for data centre build
stories.summary: A global index shows Sydney and Melbourne still trail Asian hubs, though Melbourne’s indicative build cost is slightly lower at $10.58 per watt.
stories.title_zh: Melbourne 数据中心建设成本低于 Sydney
stories.content:
Wed, 4th Nov 2026 (Today)
Turner & Townsend has found that Melbourne is cheaper than Sydney for data centre construction, with both cities ranking well below major Asian hubs including Tokyo, Hong Kong and Singapore in its latest global index.

The 2026 Data Centre Construction Index ranked Sydney 41st and Melbourne 45th out of 62 markets, with indicative construction costs of $10.74 per watt and $10.58 per watt respectively, based on a typical 60 MW design. Auckland ranked 17th at $12.69 per watt, making it the most expensive of the three Australia and New Zealand cities surveyed.

The research drew on more than 500 live or recently completed projects and a survey of more than 400 industry experts. It found global data centre construction costs continued to rise as AI-driven demand increased pressure on land, power, materials and labour.

Across Asia Pacific, Tokyo topped the global table for the fourth consecutive year at $18.28 per watt, followed by Osaka at $17.15. Singapore ranked fourth at $15.39 per watt, Hong Kong 14th at $12.97 and Jakarta 26th at $11.96.

The gap between Australia and these higher-cost hubs reflects differences in contractor depth, supply chains and project volumes, the index found. Sydney and Melbourne benefit from deeper supply chains, a larger pool of experienced contractors and a steady pipeline of projects, helping contain costs relative to some regional peers.

### Cost pressures

Even so, the report said Australia should not be seen as a low-cost market, citing ongoing competition for suitable land and constraints on available power.

Power emerged as one of the main constraints globally. Among respondents, 56% identified it as a major obstacle to successful delivery, while 52% said utility connections typically take one to two years and 32% reported timeframes of more than two years.

Labour shortages also remained a major issue. The survey found 81% of respondents said skilled labour in their region was either moderately or highly constrained, while only 52% believed contractor capacity was manageable for now.

Inflation remained uneven across the sector. More than half of respondents, 52%, said they experienced cost increases above 6% in 2026, and about one in five reported inflation above 15%.

Looking ahead, respondents indicated some easing in cost pressures, though not a return to earlier market conditions. For 2027, 28% expect inflation to be between 1% and 5%, while 57% expect it to remain below 15%.

### AI demand

The report linked much of the current construction activity to larger facilities being built for AI workloads. It said these projects require different delivery approaches, more technical specialists and contracting models that account for higher risks and tighter schedules.

Half of those surveyed expect data centres to make up most of their project pipeline next year. Specifically, 52% said most of their 2027 projects would be data centres supporting AI workloads.

Simon Kearney, Data Centre Lead, ANZ, at Turner & Townsend, said: "Fundamentally, on the back of strong economies, established supply chains and stable grid connections, Australia and New Zealand remain very attractive markets for investors. That said, each city is different.

"New Zealand's market is smaller, so there are fewer specialist contractors and less competition for work. Most major plant and equipment has to be shipped in over long distances, and strict design standards add cost. Skilled labour is also in short supply, which pushes rates up. That partly explains why Auckland is ranked 17th on this year's index.

"Sydney and Melbourne benefit from deeper supply chains, a larger pool of experienced contractors and a steady pipeline of projects, all of which helps control costs. That does not make Australia a low-cost option, though. Power constraints and competition for suitable land remain real pressures there too.

"As demand continues to accelerate, organisations that take a proactive approach to site selection, procurement and supply chain engagement will be best placed to manage delivery risk and bring capacity online faster."

Outside Asia Pacific, Zurich ranked third globally at $15.93 per watt, followed by Silicon Valley at $15.01 and Copenhagen at $14.41. Turner & Townsend said the concentration of high-cost markets in Europe and North America reflected the continued dominance of those regions, which account for around half of global data centres in North America and about a quarter in Europe.

At the other end of the ranking, Shanghai was the lowest-cost market in the index at $5.79 per watt, followed by Mumbai at $6.83 and Ho Chi Minh City at $8.32. Bogota and the UAE completed the bottom five at $9.13 and $9.20 respectively.

Paul Barry, Data Centre Construction Cost Index Lead at Turner & Townsend, said: "Over the decade since we first published our construction cost index, we have seen the data centre industry completely transformed, with capital expenditure on data centres now at US$800 billion per year and expected to reach US$1.8 trillion by 2050. AI's exponential demand for computing power, combined with cloud adoption and the growing importance of data and sovereign capacity, is driving data centre investment and development at unprecedented scale, reshaping the construction landscape.

"However, rising material and labour costs continue to create challenges globally, while access to power, specialist equipment and skills continues to create bottlenecks. Data centres are also subject to increasing scrutiny, with political and community consent essential to delivery. AI-driven demand for gigawatt-level power and liquid cooling for increased rack densities is driving the growth of larger-scale data centres, but shortages of skilled labour and the greater risks involved in delivering larger, more complex projects are creating a cost premium."

stories.content:
The stock has more than doubled so far this year

AMD forecast fourth-quarter revenue above Wall Street estimates on Tuesday (Nov 3), buoyed by strong demand for its chips as its multibillion-dollar effort to challenge Nvidia’s dominance of the AI semiconductor market gains momentum.

Shares of the company jumped over 7.5 per cent in extended trading. The stock has more than doubled so far this year. Intel shares rose 2 per cent, Nvidia stock climbed over 1 per cent and Broadcom also advanced 1.2 per cent.

AMD, which nearly doubled its data-centre revenue in the third quarter, is benefiting as a shift in AI workloads toward running models in real-world applications drives demand for its graphics processing units and central processors.

This has enabled AMD to capture market share from rival Intel, which last week forecast quarterly revenue well below estimates and triggered a global selloff in chip stocks.

AMD expects fourth-quarter revenue of about US$17 billion, plus or minus 3 per cent, above analysts’ average estimate of US$16.23 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG.

The company’s adjusted gross margin is expected to be about 55 per cent, in line with estimates of 55.27 per cent and down from 56 per cent in the third quarter.

AMD has stepped up AI product rollouts, moving beyond standalone chips to compete with Nvidia’s rack-scale systems.

The company’s flagship Helios rack, combining its MI455X accelerator and new “Venice” server chips, is in production and set for a larger ramp-up in the fourth quarter. The initial systems are being tested at Meta.

In February, the company agreed to sell up to US$60 billion worth of AI chips to Meta over five years in a deal that allows the Facebook owner to purchase as much as 10 per cent of the chip firm.

AMD’s third-quarter revenue rose 45 per cent to US$13.38 billion, beating estimates of US$13.09 billion. Data-centre revenue jumped 97 per cent to a record US$8.55 billion, exceeding estimates of US$8.20 billion.

Adjusted profit came in at US$2.09 per share, compared with estimates of US$1.95.

The semiconductor industry is also grappling with a global memory shortage, leaving expensive high-bandwidth memory used in AI processors in scarce supply as manufacturers race to increase production.

Third-quarter sales in AMD’s client and gaming segment, home to its PC chips and console processors, fell 8 per cent to US$3.72 billion, missing estimates of US$3.79 billion.

Beyond chips, AMD in September agreed to buy Fei-Fei Li’s World Labs, a startup building AI that models 3D environments, for US$8.2 billion in stock, gaining a foothold in research on physical AI systems. REUTERS

stories.title_zh: 液冷技术对数据中心测量标准提出新要求
stories.content:
The data centre industry has embraced liquid cooling, particularly direct-to-chip systems, for high-density AI workloads.Operating these facilities reliably requires a categorically different operational environment, demanding new expertise across power, structural and mechanical engineering, fluid dynamics, chemistry, and instrumentation.
### The Measurement Shift

Liquid cooling significantly extends the domain of environmental management beyond traditional air-cooled facilities.While pipes carrying cold water have always been part of data centre infrastructure, bringing cooling directly to chips through Coolant Distribution Units (CDUs) and cold plates changes the scope and criticality of liquid-side measurement.Parameters now requiring dedicated instrumentation include liquid temperature, pressure, flow rate, and level, alongside leak detection and coolant health indicators such as pH, turbidity, conductivity, and refractive index.Air-side management remains essential for managing residual heat, requiring operators to understand both environments together.
### Dew Point and Dynamic Workloads

Dew point is a critical risk area, as colder piping in an air-conditioned space can lead to condensation if pipe surface temperature drops below ambient dew point.A common practice is to maintain coolant supply temperatures at least 2°C above the measured ambient dew point.The dynamic nature of AI workloads, which can shift from idle to full load in minutes, demands real-time and accurate measurements for continuous cooling control.Reliable measurement enables precise control, helps facilities achieve efficiency targets, and provides early warnings for potential issues.Without trustworthy measurements, a liquid-cooled data centre operates on assumptions, increasing risks for both cooling infrastructure and compute hardware as architectures become more complex.

stories.title: Vertiv: From PUE to Tokenomics, AI Factory scorecard is being rewritten
stories.summary: 当AI从模型竞赛走进算力基建竞赛，一座AI Factory到底值不值钱，正在被重新定义。过去十年，人们习惯用机柜数量、装机规模来判断一座数据中心的价值，用PUE判断它是否高效。但一个更直接的问题已经摆到所有建设者面前：同样投入100MW的合同电力，究竟能换来多少真正可用的AI产出？
stories.title_zh: 维谛技术（Vertiv）：从PUE到Tokenomics，AI Factory的计分牌正在重写
stories.content:
当AI从模型竞赛走进算力基建竞赛，一座AI Factory到底值不值钱，正在被重新定义。过去十年，人们习惯用机柜数量、装机规模来判断一座数据中心的价值，用PUE判断它是否高效。但一个更直接的问题已经摆到所有建设者面前：同样投入100MW的合同电力，究竟能换来多少真正可用的AI产出？

近日，在 2026 全球计算大会（CGC）主论坛上，维谛技术（Vertiv）大中华区市场营销及产品应用部副总裁田军博士以《Tokenomics——从经济新视角，如何通过基础设施优化，实现每MW合同电力的最大AI产出》为题发表演讲，提出了衡量AI基础设施经济效益的新框架——Tokenomics：以每个合同MW能产生多少有效AI输出（Token）来量化投资回报，把物理基础设施的性能，直接映射到AI工厂的商业价值。

在他看来，PUE衡量的是“电浪费了多少”，而Tokenomics衡量的是“电变成了多少有效算力产出”。从前者到后者，是AI基础设施建设逻辑的一次根本转向。

### 合同电力并不等于算力电力：一座园区要穿过五道关口

判断一座AI Factory的真实产出，要先从电力说起。

从合同电力出发，电并不直接进入算力，而要在不同环节被多次“打折”：并网与接入限制、限电和场地就绪，让可交付的站点电力先缩水一部分；冗余预留、拓扑裕量和配电开销，再让设施可用电力退一步；制冷、排热、水泵、风机、照明与控制，又占用掉一笔可观的设施负载；电能转换损耗、网络、CPU、内存与服务器风扇，继续从关键IT电力上切走一块；走到最后，热降频、运行不稳定、停机与维护降额，还会让额定GPU电力再打一次折。

层层递减之后，真正留给有效算力的电力，已经明显低于当初签下的合同容量。名义上的装机规模与最终在产出Token的算力，中间隔着一整条会持续漏损的链路。

而这五道关口里，只有“制冷与配电”这一段，是PUE能够看见的。所以田军博士强调，真正值得算清楚的，不只是电消耗了多少，而是——从政府获得的电力容量，究竟有多少真正变成了AI生产力。

### 同样的兆瓦，不同的产出：差距不在芯片里

如果说电力在传输与转换中损耗惊人，那么Token产出效率的差距更值得深究。

田军博士给出了一组对比：同样是合同电力、同样规模的GPU集群，行业中位水平与行业领先水平，在设施可用电力、关键IT电力到有效GPU电力上的逐级留存并不相同，留在算力端的电力差距尤其突出；折算到产出端，每兆瓦每秒能跑出的Token数量以及每天每兆瓦对应的算力价值，领先者都明显高出一截。

也就是说，同样的电力投入，最终产出相差悬殊。这道差距不产生在芯片里，而产生在从电力接入到算力输出的整条基础设施链路——同样的电，进去的方式不同，出来的算力就不同。

为了把这道账算清楚，Tokenomics覆盖全链路经济产出，用四个核心指标回答客户最关心的问题：Tokens per Second是有效吞吐，衡量算力的最大产出能力；Tokens per Watt是能源生产率，衡量有限电力能换来多少产出；Tokens per Dollar是经济生产率，衡量每一美元能创造多少Token；Time to First Token是收入速度，衡量从签约到首个Token产出需要多久。

四个指标最终收束为一个终极指标：每兆瓦每秒，能产出多少Token。

### 把每一级漏损收回来：系统融合，才是 Token 价值的放大器

让每一MW电力创造更多Token，答案并不是简单增加设备，也不是单独提升某个环节的效率。因为决定AI Factory最终产出的，是从电力接入到算力运行的整个系统。

对应前文的漏损链路，抓手其实清晰。在供电架构上，通过800 VDC架构减少转换级数，以 UPS功率平滑和故障穿越稳住负载，用MV BESS UPS应对AI脉冲负载，把冗余预留与转换环节丢掉的那部分电力尽量收回来；在热管理上，以更高水温的液冷运行、热链路系统级优化，把设施负载与热降频带来的损失收回来；在交付与复制上，用工厂预制、数字化验证的参考设计，以及电力、制冷与IT的一体化交付，压缩Time to First Token，堵住接口处的容量泄漏。

由此可见，只有从单点优化走向系统协同，才能让每一环节的改善，转化为整个AI Factory的产出价值。这也正是维谛技术（Vertiv）“全融合物理基础设施”理念的核心所在。同时，这一理念已经落地为具体的基础设施解决方案——Vertiv™ OneCore全融合基础设施解决方案，通过供电、制冷与IT基础设施的集成化设计，以及预制化、模块化的交付方式，减少传统现场集成的复杂性，为AI Factory的快速部署和规模化复制提供支持。

### 不再拼 MW，而是拼 Token：AI Factory的下一场竞赛

站在产业视角，AI Factory的竞争正在从规模走向效率。

当密度、速度、规模、复杂度与负载特性五股力量叠加，传统“现场拼装、子系统逐个优化”的方式已经跟不上GW级建设的节奏。Tokenomics提供的，正是一种从投入走向产出的新视角——从关注建了多少MW，到关注产出了多少Token。

电力，正在成为AI时代最稀缺的生产要素。谁能让每一瓦电力更充分地转化为有效算力，谁就掌握了下一轮竞争的主动权。当衡量标准从“电有没有被浪费”转向“电变成了多少有效产出”，改变的不仅是评价方式，更是整个AI基础设施的设计逻辑。

从“建得出MW”到“产得出Token”，维谛技术（Vertiv）凭借前瞻视野和完整产品线优势，正以“全融合物理基础设施”理念，驱动AI Factory高效释放Token生产力。

KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 3): MM Computer Systems Bhd (KL:MMCS) said it has secured a purchase order worth RM51.58 million to supply graphics processing unit (GPU)-accelerated servers.

“This contract underscores MMCS’s capabilities in delivering advanced IT infrastructure solutions amid growing demand for AI and high-performance computing technologies,” MMCS said in a statement on Tuesday.

The IT solutions provider did not disclose the name of the party that awarded the contract to its wholly owned subsidiary, Micro Technology Solution Sdn Bhd, saying only that it is a Malaysian telecommunications infrastructure and data centre services provider.

MMCS said the servers are designed to support computationally intensive workloads, including generative AI, large language model training and inference, deep learning, advanced data analytics and high-performance computing.

The company expects the contract to contribute positively to its earnings and net assets per share.

MMCS shares closed unchanged at 36.5 sen on Tuesday, valuing the company at RM207 million. The stock, which debuted on the ACE Market in June, has risen over 65% from its initial public offering price of 22 sen.

stories.summary: NTT Data has launched its JKT2A data center in Indonesia, expanding the company's footprint in Southeast Asia's largest economy. The facility adds capacity in Jakarta, where demand for digital infrastructure is rising rapidly among local enterprises and international cloud providers.

stories.title_zh: NTT Data 在印尼开设 JKT2A data center
stories.summary_zh: NTT Data 已在其位于印度尼西亚的 JKT2A data center 投入运营，扩大了该公司在东南亚最大经济体的业务布局。该设施增加了雅加达的容量，当地企业和国际 cloud 提供商对数字基础设施的需求正在快速增长。

stories.content:
NTT Data has opened its Jakarta 2 Annex Data Center (JKT2A) in Indonesia.

The 12MW facility, which is part of NTT’s Jakarta Campus. NTT said the facility uses advanced cooling technologies and will support hyperscale, enterprise, and high-density workloads.

Plans for JKT2A were announced in May 2024. The seven-story facility covers 5,800 sqm (62,430 sq ft), with rack densities of up to 40kW.

Alongside the opening, NTT also launched APN Connect, which it says is the first service in Indonesia to use All-Photonics Network technology. APN Connect will provide low-latency connectivity between JKT2A and JKT3. NTT said the service will allow for real-time data synchronization between facilities.

“The opening of JKT2A is an important milestone for our business in Indonesia and, more importantly, for the many clients we serve here,” said Yasuhiro Kajiki, managing director, Japan and APAC for NTT Global Data Centers. “By expanding our capacity and connecting the facilities through APN Connect, we are creating a more connected and resilient data center platform that gives our clients greater flexibility as their infrastructure needs evolve. We are proud to continue investing in Indonesia’s digital future.”

“Indonesia is one of the most dynamic digital economies in Southeast Asia, and it is creating significant demand for scalable, highly connected digital infrastructure,” said Doug Adams, president and CEO, NTT Global Data Centers. “The opening of JKT2A reflects our ongoing commitment to supporting clients’ cloud, AI and digital transformation initiatives with resilient, high-performance infrastructure. Together with APN Connect, JKT2A strengthens our ability to deliver the scale, connectivity and reliability organizations need to accelerate innovation and growth.”

stories.title: Samsung SDS breaks ground on Gumi AI Data Center in South Korea
stories.summary: Samsung SDS has broken ground on its Gumi AI Data Center in South Korea, marking a significant expansion of the Samsung group's AI infrastructure capabilities. The facility is designed to support high-performance computing workloads and will leverage Samsung's advanced semiconductor and memory technologies.
stories.why_it_matters: South Korea's government and chaebols are racing to build domestic AI capacity amid geopolitical tensions over chip access, with Samsung uniquely positioned to optimize vertically integrated facilities using its own HBM, SSD, and foundry output. This buildout intensifies competition with SK Telecom's AI data center plans and may reduce Korean enterprises' reliance on foreign cloud providers for sensitive workloads.
stories.title_zh: Samsung SDS 在韩国龟尾市动工建设 Gumi AI Data Center
stories.summary_zh: Samsung SDS 已在其位于韩国的 Gumi AI Data Center 破土动工，标志着 Samsung 集团 AI 基础设施能力的重大扩展。该设施旨在支持高性能计算工作负载，并将利用 Samsung 先进的半导体和内存技术。
stories.why_zh: 在芯片获取的地缘政治紧张局势下，韩国政府和财阀正竞相建设国内 AI 能力，而 Samsung 凭借自身 HBM、SSD 和代工产出，在优化垂直整合设施方面具有独特优势。这一建设加剧了与 SK Telecom AI data center 计划的竞争，并可能减少韩国企业在敏感工作负载上对外国 cloud 提供商的依赖。
stories.content:
Samsung SDS has broken ground on a new AI data center in Gongdan-dong, Gumi-Si, South Korea.

Dubbed the Gumi AI Data Center, the facility will be developed in phases, starting with 60MW of capacity and ultimately scaling to 120MW.

The data center will be housed on a 498,165 sq ft (46,281 sqm) site. With construction now underway, the data center is expected to be completed in late 2028.

The data center project is part of Samsung's commitment to invest 60 trillion won ($44.671bn) in establishing the Yeongnam region as a "Global Physical AI Innovation Cluster." Samsung SDS announced last January that it would invest 427.3 billion ($318 million) in an AI data center in Gumi, and signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with North Gyeongsang Province and Gumi City for the construction of the project.

The company is also investing in manufacturing and robot automation, all-solid-state batteries, package substrates for AI servers, and MLCCs (Multilayer Ceramic Capacitors).

The data center will have a hybrid cooling system, combining air cooling in general server areas for networking and storage, and liquid cooling for the high-density GPU server areas.

The data center will host in-house GPUs that can offer compute to customers, but will also have a colocation business to host other companies' hardware.

Lee Jun-hee, president and CEO of Samsung SDS, said: "AI is transforming the way companies work and the competitiveness of industries. For these changes to translate into tangible results, a robust foundation capable of processing vast amounts of data and operating AI stably is required, and the Gumi AI Data Center will fulfill that role."

He added: "Samsung SDS will combine its accumulated experience in data center construction and operation with its cloud and AI technology capabilities to create an AI infrastructure that customers can trust and utilize."

Samsung SDS is the IT and cloud unit of Samsung. In August 2026, it revealed it would be launching an NPU-as-a-Service (NPUaaS) offering in South Korea with FuriosaAI's RNGD NPUs.

Samsung SDS is deploying the RNGD accelerators at its data center in Dongtan, which opened in March 2023. Named Dongtan IDC, the data center spans six floors with four server rooms, and has a PUE of 1.12 enabled by its use of natural air cooling.

Samsung SDS claims to operate 18 data centers from which it offers cloud services, and with the Gumi site, it will have five in South Korea.

stories.title: Foxconn details quantum ambitions, wants to become world's largest quantum computer manufacturer
stories.summary: Foxconn wants to become the world’s largest manufacturer of quantum computing systems, chairman Young Liu has said.
stories.title_zh: Foxconn 阐述量子雄心，欲成为全球最大的 quantum computer 制造商
stories.content:
Foxconn wants to become the world’s largest manufacturer of quantum computing systems, chairman Young Liu has said.

Speaking during an interview with CNBC, Liu said the company had identified an opportunity to work with quantum hardware companies to produce quantum computers without entering the market itself.

“We focus on manufacturing,” Liu said. “We hope we can become the largest quantum computer manufacturer in the world without owning that technology.”

However, when asked when quantum computing will become “commercially viable,” Liu said he believed it would be at least another two years, not just for Foxconn but for the whole industry.

Liu added that while quantum hardware would never replace CPUs or GPUs, there was a clear requirement for quantum computing for certain problems and workloads that “are very difficult for the classical computer to solve because it takes a much longer period of time.”

He added: “I would not say that will be the next revolutionary computing devices. It will be a new addition to the compute devices with a special function that accelerates certain computations.”

Taiwanese manufacturer Foxconn, officially known as Hon Hai Technology Group, made a name for itself manufacturing iPhones but emerged as one of the big winners of the AI boom, becoming the largest producer of Nvidia servers.

In August 2025, the company announced that it had generated more revenue from the production and sale of servers than it did from its consumer electronics division for the first time in company history.

stories.content:
A new data center has launched in Jakarta, Indonesia.

SM+ this week announced the opening of SMX01, a new facility in the Indonesian capital focused on providing AI capacity.

“SMX01 has officially commenced operations on 1 November 2026, adding 21MW of AI-ready data center capacity to Indonesia’s digital infrastructure landscape,” the company said on LinkedIn.

Located in Jakarta’s central business district, the carrier-neutral SMX01 features four network entry points and offers liquid-cooling capabilities alongside conventional air-cooling systems.

The $300 million data center was first announced in September 2024 as a joint venture between LG Sinar Mas, SM+ Data Centers, and Korea Investment Real Asset Management. Construction started in March 2025.

The company previously said the data center is set to have a total capacity of 27MW with a first-phase target of 6MW. SMX01 will support high-density workloads, with up to 130kW per rack.

Taiwanese cloud and AI infrastructure provider Konst is leasing capacity at the facility. On LinkedIn, the company said it has taken on 15MW of liquid-cooled capacity at SMX01. It is the company’s first deployment in Indonesia.

LG Sinar Mas is a 50:50 joint venture between LG CNS, a South Korean data center and IT services company, and SM+.

Jakarta-based SM+ is a digital infrastructure and services platform backed by local conglomerate Sinar Mas and founded in 2023. It has two divisions: SM+ Data Centers owns and operates 25 data centers across Indonesia, amounting to some 40MW of operational and under-development IT load capacity. SM+ Technology Solutions, meanwhile, operates as an IT service provider and systems integrator.

Founded in 2024, Taiwanese cloud provider and AI infrastructure company Konst is headquartered in Nangang, Taipei. Its operations include GPU data center construction, GPU cloud services, bare-metal leasing, colocation services, and AI infrastructure. stories.title: Anthropic S-1 update reveals $895.4bn in cloud and data center commitments
stories.summary: Anthropic has amended its Form S-1 filing with the SEC, adding details on the latest quarter's earnings.
stories.title_zh: Anthropic S-1更新显示8954亿美元云计算和数据中心承诺
stories.content:
Anthropic has amended its Form S-1 filing with the SEC, adding details on the latest quarter's earnings.

Ahead of an imminent public listing, the company disclosed Q3 results of $17 billion in revenue, up about 1,127 percent over last year. However, revenue growth slowed on a quarter-to-quarter basis to 47 percent - down from 144 percent growth in Q2 and 132 percent in Q1.

Anthropic also reported a net loss of $23.29bn in its third quarter.

Also updated were its financial commitments, previously listed at $417bn for compute. Now, the company said its purchase commitments and lease agreements have an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion, “substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure.”

The company's compute and infrastructure expenses increased to $14.4bn for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up 329 percent over last year.

Anthropic is expected to have more than 3.5GW of compute this year, the New York Times reports, with a similar amount due in 2027.

According to its prospectus, it has committed $121.3bn to lease compute from Google, $120.5bn from SpaceX, $110bn from Amazon, and $44.9bn from Microsoft.

The deals with Google, Amazon, and Microsoft are mostly non-cancelable outside of uncured material breaches, and must be paid regardless of actual usage. The SpaceX deal is cancelable with 90 days' notice from next March.

In addition to the Google deal, Anthropic is set to procure additional TPU compute, either through a Google Cloud deal, a direct purchase from Google with five-year financing, or through a partner. That compute, expected between 2028 and 2031, could cost $125-150bn, and is not a part of the $895bn calculation.

Outside of the hyperscalers, Anthropic has signed a $44.6bn deal with neocloud Nscale until 2033 and $41.3bn with Lambda until 2034. However, Nscale is required to try to obtain qualifying financing for its Nvidia GPUs, while Lambda will have to secure its facility lease in a timely manner.

It has also entered into a $50 billion deal with Fluidstack, as well as contracts with TeraWulf and Hut 8.

Anthropic did not mention its $11.6bn cloud deal with Akamai, nor its compute agreement with CoreWeave.

The prospectus also reiterated its hardware supply agreement with AMD, where the chip designer is on track to buy $5bn in Anthropic shares. That will happen in stages, based on AMD GPU delivery and deployment milestones.

Anthropic's Australian subsidiary has signed a lease agreement with Australian Data Centres (ADC).

He added: "Further details will be provided at financial close of the Anthropic project.

Ross also described ADC as a "small Australian data center business." According to ADC's website, the company has two data centers in Canberra that are operational, located in Mitchell and Fyshwick. Locations in Melbourne, Sydney, and Darwin are "in development," and Adelaide, Perth, and Brisbane are "in planning." The Canberra site was acquired in December 2025.

Details about the deal with Anthropic were not provided, but reports in September suggested that the consortium also includes Zerra DC, and will be for four data centers on 720 hectares of land in Dalby, northwest of Queensland. The data centers are expected to offer 2.16GW of capacity and be the first to go online in 2027.
