stories.title: Vietnam's domestic chip push gains ground as Viettel, FPT unveil new capabilities
stories.summary: Viettel launches domestically designed security chip platform; FPT starts trial operations at testing plant
stories.title_zh: Viettel和FPT发布新能力，越南本土chip推进取得进展
stories.content:
Viettel launches domestically designed security chip platform; FPT starts trial operations at testing plant

VIETNAM’S Viettel Group and FPT Corporation unveiled new semiconductor design and testing capabilities on Tuesday (Nov 3), marking progress in the South-east Asian nation’s efforts to build a domestic chip industry and reduce its dependence on foreign technology.

Military-run Viettel and the Government Cipher Committee (GCC) unveiled what they described as Vietnam’s first domestically developed security semiconductor platform, alongside a security chip built using a mature 28-nanometre manufacturing process.

Separately, FPT began trial operations at a semiconductor testing facility in northern Bac Ninh province – about 30 km north-east of Hanoi – with a maximum designed capacity of 300 million chips annually.

The developments highlight efforts by Vietnamese companies to expand their presence across different stages of the semiconductor supply chain, from chip design to testing and packaging.

This is as the government seeks to strengthen domestic capabilities in a strategically important industry still dominated by foreign-invested firms.

Earlier in January, Viettel and FPT announced plans to jointly develop artificial intelligence chips for cameras, drones and other smart devices, as part of a broader partnership spanning semiconductor design, manufacturing, testing and packaging.

Viettel is also developing what is intended to be Vietnam’s first domestic semiconductor wafer fabrication plant in Hanoi, with trial production targeted for 2027 and full operations by 2030.

## Security chips for strategic applications

Viettel’s security chip, known as VGC v1.0, incorporates Vietnamese-developed cryptographic algorithms directly into its hardware, allowing sensitive data to be encrypted and decrypted without relying solely on software.

The approach is intended to strengthen domestic control over sensitive data security, and address concerns about potential vulnerabilities associated with imported chips.

The chip, containing 300 million transistors and housed in a 10 by 10 mm package, is designed for government and defence applications. Its developers said tests showed it could encrypt and decrypt data about 15 times faster than a software-only solution performing the same tasks.

The chip has already been deployed in secure USB storage devices used by government and defence agencies, the company said. Viettel plans to expand its use to applications supporting Vietnam’s national digital signature certification system, which currently has more than two million digital certificates in circulation.

Meanwhile, the security semiconductor platform, developed jointly by Viettel and GCC, uses the open-standard RISC-V instruction set architecture. This allows Vietnamese engineers to independently design and modify processors while retaining control over core design and verification processes.

Viettel said its engineers had also developed safeguards to protect the chip design before transferring it to a semiconductor foundry, to reduce the risk of information leakage and reverse engineering.

Viettel and GCC also signed an agreement on Tuesday to develop plans for volume production of VGC v1.0 and work on a multicore security chip platform incorporating dedicated cryptographic components. The partnership also covers technical testing and training semiconductor engineers.

Viettel plans to expand its semiconductor design capabilities to develop chips for both civilian and military applications, including AI, 6G telecommunications, smart cameras, drones and robotics, as part of efforts to reduce Vietnam’s reliance on imported semiconductors.

“Being a latecomer does not mean accepting dependence on others,” Viettel chairman and CEO Tao Duc Thang said.

“With the right strategy, focused resources and sustained commitment, we can progressively close the gap and ultimately gain control over technologies of strategic importance to our country.”

In October 2023, Viettel unveiled its first domestically designed 5G digital front-end chip, designed to handle signal processing and control functions in 5G base stations.

## Building domestic testing capacity

Meanwhile, FPT’s new testing facility builds on its existing semiconductor design capabilities, including the development of specialised chips for Internet of Things and AI applications.

This is as the company seeks to expand its presence across the chip value chain and strengthen Vietnam’s role in global semiconductor supply chains.

The 1,600 sq m testing facility at Yen Phong II-C Industrial Park features six testing lines equipped with automated systems to assess chip functionality, quality and reliability.

FPT expects to undertake its first chip-testing order for a South Korean partner during the initial operating phase, aiming to serve both domestic and international semiconductor companies.

The company said its engineers are developing customised testing programmes for different chip designs and researching the use of AI to automate testing processes. It also plans to expand into more advanced testing and packaging technologies.

The new facility is expected to support workforce development as well, with practical training programmes for students planned from December.

## The missing piece: wafer fabrication

Vietnam has emerged as a growing hub for semiconductor design, assembly, testing and packaging, with chip-design operations by companies including Marvell Technology, Synopsys and Renesas Electronics.

These are alongside major assembly and testing investments from US-based Intel and Amkor Technology, as well as South Korea’s Hana Micron.

More recently, Samsung Electronics outlined plans to invest up to US$4.1 billion in memory-chip testing facilities, while its affiliate Samsung Electro-Mechanics announced a US$1.9 billion expansion of semiconductor substrate production.

LG Innotek is also developing a US$1 billion semiconductor substrate plant in the northern port city of Hai Phong.

However, Vietnam has yet to house a semiconductor wafer fabrication plant.

Citing people familiar with the matter, Reuters reported on Oct 26 that Viettel’s US$1.3 billion semiconductor fabrication plant was unlikely to meet its 2027 target, with construction yet to begin and negotiations over lithography equipment from Dutch supplier ASML still unresolved.

Viettel, however, maintained that the project was progressing according to schedule.

The Ministry of Science and Technology said that as at late 2025, Vietnam had about 60 chip design companies, eight semiconductor packaging and testing projects, and more than 20 suppliers of semiconductor materials and equipment.

Under its national semiconductor strategy, Vietnam aims to expand its ecosystem to at least 100 chip design companies, one small-scale fabrication plant, and 10 packaging and testing facilities by 2030.

Longer-term targets for 2050 include 300 design companies, three fabrication plants and 20 packaging and testing facilities. THE BUSINESS TIMES

stories.title: Grid delays, local opposition slow data center expansion
stories.summary: Data center projects face extended development timelines due to grid connection delays and local opposition, complicating expansion plans. This impacts the ability to meet growing demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure.
stories.title_zh: 电网延迟和地方反对减缓数据中心扩张
stories.content:
Data center projects are experiencing longer development timelines as operators work to secure electricity connections and local approvals, according to Data Center Knowledge.This trend complicates expansion plans for artificial intelligence (AI)-related capacity. Projects that began construction between the third quarter of 2025 and the third quarter of 2026 waited over two years after announcement.This compares with approximately 18 months for projects that started construction between early 2020 and mid-2025, GlobalData reported. Martina Raveni, a senior analyst on GlobalData’s Strategic Intelligence team, noted that grid access and public opposition are the two primary constraints.She stated that new grid infrastructure can take five to 15 years to build, while a data center takes one to three years. GlobalData forecasts annual data center electricity consumption will increase from 590 terawatt-hours (TWh) in 2025 to 1,520 TWh in 2030.Meeting this demand requires developers to address power, permitting, and construction bottlenecks. Luis Fernandes, IDC senior research manager for cloud and data centers, identified grid access as the dominant obstacle, halting entire projects.Community resistance, driven by concerns over electricity bills, water consumption, noise, and land use, also affects permitting and construction schedules. Ya-Han Brownlee-Chen, DP World’s vice president of data center strategy in the Americas, highlighted growing tension between AI infrastructure demand and community willingness to host facilities.Developers can use on-site gas generation as an alternative to delayed grid connections, but this can intensify local resistance due to environmental concerns. Joe Johnston, Xylem executive vice president, called for more efficient water and cooling infrastructure to support expansion.The effect on AI development remains unclear. Raveni noted capacity rationing by cloud providers and earlier reservations for customers. Fernandes, however, found no hard evidence that compute capacity limitations are currently hindering AI development.He attributed rising computing costs more to material shortages, including memory supplies for high-end graphics processing unit (GPU) manufacturing. Developers must establish credible power and construction schedules while engaging early and transparently with communities on concerns like electricity bills and water use.

stories.content:
LG CNS, a South Korean digital transformation company, targets North American and European expansion with modular data center strategy. Its US subsidiary will work with local partners with an initial 30 MW of power capacity, expandable to 220 MW.

The company’s prefabricated modular approach involves manufacturing key data center components in advance and assembling them on site, thus reducing construction time. LG CNS sees the model as a way to address development delays linked to power constraints and shortages of skilled workers as reported by ajupress.

Yoo Ki-woong, vice president, AI and cloud division, LG CNS, said during an earnings call on Friday: “We plan to step up our push into North America and Europe based on our prefabricated modular data center capabilities and supply chain built on Nvidia’s Vera Rubin.”

Readers will recall that LG CNS has recently completed construction of a 30 MW AI data center in Jakarta, Indonesia. The project was commissioned by Kuningan Mas Gemilang (KMG), a joint venture between Indonesia’s Cinarmas Group and South Korea’s Tuzarial Asset Management.

The facility is designed to support high performance computing (HPC) using next generation graphics processing units (GPUs) and marks the first time a South Korean company has directly built an AI data center overseas for a local customer.

stories.summary_zh: 据《金融时报》报道，Nvidia 正施压其 data centre 合作伙伴限制与中国客户的业务往来。这一指令出台之际，美国政府正收紧对中国先进 AI 芯片的出口管制，Nvidia 此前已不得不推出降级版 GPU 以符合法规要求。

stories.content:
SAN FRANCISCO (Nov 3): US chipmaking giant Nvidia is ordering its data centre partners to scale back work with Chinese customers, the *Financial Times* (*FT*) reported on Tuesday.

Nvidia's cloud computing clients must now sell at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese companies, the *FT* reported, citing five people with knowledge of the matter.

The new rules only affect future contracts and not existing agreements, the report said.

Nvidia neither confirmed nor denied the report to *AFP*, but said in a statement that "data centres and clouds built on American chips are the foundation that American model and application makers need to compete worldwide".

"Long-standing US policy encourages every cloud to build on American infrastructure and to win business everywhere they can," the statement said.

"America cannot win the AI race unless America's AI infrastructure wins worldwide. If the world's clouds rely on foreign-made chips, the model and application layers will be foreign-built as well."

Asked about the report, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said she was not aware of it.

"As a matter of principle, we consistently hope that all parties can provide a fair, transparent and non-discriminatory business environment for companies from all countries, including Chinese companies," she said.

China and the US are locked in a race for dominance in the fast-moving artificial intelligence (AI) sector.

In recent months, the two countries have traded accusations of stealing AI technologies and jeopardising security.

Nvidia is the world's most valuable company thanks to the global drive to build data centres packed with specialist computer chips and other hardware that runs AI systems.

The projection points to sustained spending on facilities, computing equipment and infrastructure upgrades as businesses expand cloud use and integrate artificial intelligence into core processes. Demand for data storage, processing and reliable digital infrastructure is also rising alongside wider use of online services.

Operators and suppliers are responding to heavier, more complex workloads by modernising infrastructure to improve capacity use, energy efficiency and operational flexibility, while expanding support for cloud platforms, AI systems and other data-intensive applications.

### Sector demand

Healthcare, banking and retail are among the sectors driving demand as they process larger volumes of information, support digital transactions and seek uninterrupted service delivery. The shift of business operations to digital platforms is also increasing the need for scalable infrastructure that can handle growing data volumes and more demanding applications.

Edge computing and the Internet of Things are creating another layer of investment demand, prompting the construction of more distributed data centre infrastructure to support connected devices and applications that require low-latency processing.

Large data centres remained the biggest part of the market in 2025, accounting for nearly 42% of global revenue, according to the study. Mega data centres are expected to record the fastest growth over the forecast period, with a projected compound annual growth rate of 9.1% between 2026 and 2032, reflecting demand for high-capacity sites linked to hyperscale cloud services and AI workloads.

### Regional split

North America held almost 50% of the global market in 2025, supported by a well-established technology sector and mature digital infrastructure. Asia is forecast to grow faster, with a projected compound annual growth rate of 8.4% from 2026 to 2032, driven by digitalisation, wider cloud adoption and infrastructure development across regional economies.

The report also points to changing customer preferences on facility reliability. While Tier 1 and Tier 2 sites have historically been widely used, demand is shifting towards infrastructure with higher availability and stronger operational resilience.

Tier 4 data centres are expected to expand at a compound annual growth rate of 8.8% by 2032 as organisations seek to reduce the risk of service disruption and support continuous digital operations. The trend reflects businesses' growing dependence on always-on systems for customer services, transactions and internal processes.

### Cost and power

Despite the growth outlook, operators face constraints that could shape how quickly new capacity comes online. The study identifies power access, rising operating costs, environmental pressure, regulatory compliance and technology upgrades as key structural challenges for the industry.

To address those issues, companies are turning to more efficient equipment, renewable energy and new cooling methods. The report highlights airflow management measures such as hot and cold aisle optimisation as a way to improve cooling efficiency and cut energy use, while noting that cooler climates can reduce cooling demand in some locations.

Balancing computing performance, operating costs and sustainability is becoming a central issue as more workloads shift into data centres. For operators, that means expanding capacity while tightening energy management and limiting environmental effects.

Major players identified in the market include Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, IBM and Equinix. Continued enterprise migration to cloud platforms and broader AI deployment are expected to increase the importance of scalable, reliable and resource-efficient data centre solutions.

These developments are expected to support market growth at the same time encouraging innovations in operational efficiency, reliability, and performance."

stories.title: Nvidia in talks to backstop Nscale's Monarch Compute Campus project for Anthropic
stories.summary: Nvidia is said to be in talks to provide financial backing to Nscale for its 460MW data center project being developed for Anthropic.
stories.title_zh: Nvidia洽谈为Anthropic的Nscale Monarch Compute Campus项目提供支持
stories.content:
Nvidia is said to be in talks to provide financial backing to Nscale for its 460MW data center project being developed for Anthropic.

As per a report from The Information, citing people with knowledge of the deal discussions, an agreement could see Nvidia providing billions in credit guarantees for debt related to the build-out.

Nscale reportedly signed its second contract with Anthropic in October 2026. Both agreements were valued at around $45 billion, and for 460MW of capacity each at the company's upcoming Monarch Compute Campus in West Virginia.

The Monarch campus in West Virginia is Nscale's largest project, with the company acquiring the 2,250-acre site in March 2026.

The site has the potential to have up to 8GW of capacity, with the first phase planned at 2GW and expected to be online by the first half of 2028. Power will be provided by Caterpillar's fast-response natural gas generator sets – the Caterpillar G3500 series.

According to The Information, the credit support agreement would cover the power and construction for the first data center building Anthropic contracted, which will house Nvidia Vera Rubin hardware.

The Nvidia backstop is estimated to amount to more than $5bn, and would enable Nscale to secure debt for the project's buildout, with Nvidia serving as a guarantor should Nscale default on payments.

*DCD* has contacted Nscale and Nvidia for comment.

Nscale is currently preparing for its Initial Public Offering (IPO), having filed in September 2026. Later that month, the company raised $3.36 billion in private funding.

Nvidia is a major investor in several neoclouds - themselves some of the chip designer's biggest customers. The company has invested an estimated $170 billion in neoclouds and large customers, including through credit guarantees for their buildouts.

In late October, Nvidia was reportedly in talks to invest several hundred million dollars in Aussie neocloud Firmus after the company pulled out of its own IPO.

stories.title: Megaspeed exec with close ties to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang suspected of spying for China
stories.summary: An executive at Singapore-based data center firm Megaspeed has been accused of spying for China, targeting Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
stories.title_zh: 与NVIDIA CEO黄仁勋关系密切的Megaspeed高管涉嫌为中国从事间谍活动
stories.content:
An executive at Singapore-based data center firm Megaspeed has been accused of spying for China, targeting Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

Officials in the US, Singapore, and Taiwan are reportedly investigating Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen) for working on behalf of the Chinese state.

Jensen Huang has called the claims "groundless speculation," while the Chinese Embassy in Washington has rejected the allegations.

The New York Times reports that American officials concluded that Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset with a close relationship to Jensen Huang.

Megaspeed has been publicly accused of helping ship embargoed Nvidia hardware into China, including in 2025 reporting from the NYT and Bloomberg. It is also alleged to have deployed GPUs in Malaysia and Indonesia that appear to remotely serve customers in China.

At the time, Megaspeed said that it was “a Singapore-based company, operating fully in compliance with all applicable laws, including US export control regulations.” Nvidia said that its compliance teams found no untoward activity.

Megaspeed said that it had faced several government investigations and reviews. “These thorough investigations have confirmed that there has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities, and this demonstrates that we are a compliant and legitimate company,” Megaspeed said at the time.

During US surveillance of Alice Huang, it was discovered that she was in contact with an American citizen. While US intelligence agencies cannot surveil American citizens without a court order, they can argue for an 'unmasking' when citizens are in communication with surveilled individuals. In this case, the unmasking revealed communications with Jensen Huang.

When President Donald Trump was first briefed on the intelligence a year ago, US officials did not believe the Nvidia executive knew about Alice Huang's alleged information gathering for the Chinese. The US did not inform Nvidia or Jensen Huang about its suspicions.

“We’re confident that if the US government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know,” Nvidia said in a statement.

The Singapore Police Force said investigations into Megaspeed are ongoing and declined to comment further.

Following the NYT's story, Trump was asked by reporters if he still trusted Jensen Huang: “I would like to say yes. I mean, unless we find out something to the contrary.”

“I’ve always found Jensen Huang to be very aboveboard. But you know, you’re dealing in a very complex issue. We hope everything’s okay with Jensen."

Nvidia has long pushed for greater access to the Chinese market, responsible for a fifth of its sales before the US limited chip exports.

Lobbying by Nvidia and Jensen Huang, which has included private dinners with Trump and a $20m donation to the White House Ballroom, has helped reverse some of the Biden-era restrictions.

Limited quantities of Nvidia H200 GPUs are allowed to be exported to China, with the US government taking a 25 percent cut. The Chinese government has also enforced its own import restrictions on the hardware to foster domestic competition.

In March, the cofounder of server maker Supermicro, Wally Liaw, was arrested on charges of violating US export-control laws by allegedly working to smuggle $2.5 billion worth of Nvidia GPU servers into China. The company has denied wrongdoing; Liaw has pled not guilty.
